newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan central bank stays course on money policy.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan central bank stays course on money policy.

text.p: Taiwan central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong on Thursday reiterated his longstanding "stable to loose" monetary policy and attributed the Taiwan dollar's firmness against a surging U.S. dollar to local factors.

Sheu, addressing reporters after a bank board meeting convened following the currency market's close, said the central bank had no plans to intervene in the foreign exchange market and would let the Taiwan dollar find its own value.
"The central bank will let market forces determine the foreign exchange rate unless the financial market stability is affected," he said, repeating a longstanding policy stand.
He gave no explanation as to what might be seen as market instability.

Sheu said the Taiwan dollar's January push to as high as T$27.33 to the U.S. dollar -- a rise that defied the U.S. unit's remarkable appreciation against the Japanese yen -- could be attributed to what he called local "seasonal factors".

Sheu was referring to traditional demand for Taiwan dollar liquidity in the runup to the February 7 Chinese lunar new year holiday, when firms with good performance reward employees with "red packets" stuffed with year-end cash bonuses.
The Taiwan dollar rose to an intra-day high of T$27.410 against the U.S. unit on Thursday then drifted back to close at T$27.443, still a gain from Wednesday's T$27.450 close.
Sheu declined to comment further on the U.S. dollar's rise and what effect it might have on the Taiwan dollar in the absence of such local factors.

Sheu gave no hint as to what level it favoured for the local currency, though local foreigh exchange dealers have said the central bank might be eager to U.S. dollars to help maintain a stable exchange rate.
Said one dealer at a foreign bank: "It's obvious the central bank welcomes U.S. dollar selling by local exporters. We suspect the bank may also be taking part in the selling."

The U.S. dollar slipped by almost a yen in Tokyo on Thursday after vaulting on Wednesday to its highest level in just under four years amid a growing sense that Japan would tolerate the new weakened level of its currency.
Sheu's insistence that the bank would "continue its stable to loose monetary policy" indicated that its view of Taiwan's disappointingly sluggish economic recovery had not changed.

Sheu and other economic policymakers calculate that relatively easy money in the banking system holds out the best hope for speeding up the recovery without posing a significant risk of spurring inflation.

Sheu also stood firm in the face of open calls by the cabinet's policymaking Council for Economic Planning and Development to lower its official "target zone" for annual growth of the broad M2 money supply.
Sheu pledged to keep the target at 9-14 percent despite the council's appeal to bring it down to 8-13 percent.
